title: Bless the year
hook: a prayer for the year's harvest and livelihood

segments.voice: Yesterday, refuah, healing, with names added quietly. Your line was thinking of you. Today, the ninth blessing, about food, work and money.

Here's a strange fact about Jewish prayer outside the land of Israel. On a date in early December, Jews in New York, London and Buenos Aires change one line of the weekday Amidah. Not on a Jewish holiday: on a date tied to an old way of counting from the autumn equinox. In Israel the change comes weeks earlier. The line is about rain. But it sits inside a blessing about something everyone, everywhere, worries about: making a living.
screen: `A LINE CHANGES IN EARLY DECEMBER.` → `NOT ON A JEWISH HOLIDAY.` → `A BLESSING ABOUT MAKING A LIVING.`

segments.voice: The ninth blessing is called birkat hashanim, the blessing of the years. It says: bless this year for us, and all its kinds of produce, for good. Satisfy us from its goodness, and bless our year like the good years. Blessed are You, who blesses the years. In the rainy season, people ask: give dew and rain for a blessing. In the dry season, simply: give blessing. A week ago you met the rain line in Gevurot. That one praises God who makes the rain fall. This one actually asks for it. In Israel, the asking begins in the autumn, on the seventh of the month of Cheshvan; the Mishnah explains the delay: so that the last pilgrim from the festival could get home, as far as the river Euphrates, before the rain. Outside Israel, Jews follow the Babylonian Talmud's reckoning, which is why the date lands in early December. The Talmud, in Megillah 17b, also says why this blessing is ninth: against people who drive prices up, because of a line in what it counts as the ninth psalm, break the arm of the wicked. Even a blessing about harvests keeps one eye on fairness. If you don't farm, the blessing still fits. Some add their own words here about work and income, what Jews call parnassah, livelihood. Like the good years: a modest request. Not a fortune. A year that feeds you, the way the good ones did.
screen: `BIRKAT HASHANIM: BLESS THE YEARS.` · `ASKING FOR RAIN, NOT ONLY PRAISING.` · `ISRAEL IN AUTUMN, ABROAD IN DECEMBER.` · `PARNASSAH: A LIVING.` · then, large: `BLESS THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Picture your work, whatever it is, a job, a business, school, caring for kids or parents, looking for work, and the year ahead of it, the good months and the slow ones. Hold one modest hope for it: not a windfall, just a year that feeds you and the people who depend on you. If you pray, you can ask in the blessing's own words, like the good years.
Parnassah. Livelihood — what the ninth blessing, birkat hashanim, asks for alongside rain and harvest: a year that feeds you, like the good years.
Your line: a year that feeds you. Not a fortune, just the good years again. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Birkat hashanim is the ninth blessing of the weekday Amidah; Jews in Israel add the request for dew and rain from the seventh of Cheshvan, Jews elsewhere from early December, and some add personal requests for livelihood within it.

chat.says: Is it okay to pray about money? Feels a bit unspiritual.
options: Yes. The ninth blessing asks for a good year, and many add words about their work.
Only if it's for charity; asking for your own income isn't allowed.
Only farmers should ask; that blessing is only about crops and rain.

notes: Diaspora start date for ten tal umatar: the evening of December 4 or 5 (60 days after the Julian-reckoned tekufah, per Taanit 10a); confirm phrasing 'around the fourth or fifth'.
Mishnah Taanit 1:3: seventh (or fifteenth) of Cheshvan so that the last pilgrim reaches the Euphrates; confirm.

Megillah 17b: blessing of years ninth against price-raisers, with 'break Thou the arm of the wicked' said by David in the ninth psalm (Psalm 10 counted as the ninth); confirm attribution (Rabbi Alexandri).
Personal requests for parnassah within this blessing: common custom; confirm phrasing.
